title: The whole gospel in a prayer (CCC 2761)
word: The whole gospel in a prayer
hook: Tertullian called the Our Father a summary of the whole gospel

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus's prayer at the supper: John 17, the prayer of the hour. Your line was his prayer for us. Who did you remember when you heard that they all may be one? Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

Could a whole faith fit on an index card? An early Christian writer named Tertullian thought one already did. He wrote a work on prayer, and near its start he made a bold claim about the prayer Jesus taught his disciples, the Our Father. In it, he said, is a summary of the whole gospel. Not a piece of it. The whole. The Catechism opens one of its articles on the Lord's Prayer with his words. All this week it has walked through prayer from the outside: where it comes from, the way it travels, its guides, its expressions, its battles, and Jesus's own prayer at the supper. Now it opens the prayer itself. Today: the whole gospel in a prayer.
screen: `A FAITH ON AN INDEX CARD?` → `TERTULLIAN'S BOLD CLAIM.` → `THE WEEK ARRIVES AT ONE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Tertullian's words in Latin are breviarium totius evangelii: a short summary of the whole gospel. Test the claim against the prayer itself, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Then bread, forgiveness, temptation, and deliverance from evil. Now hold the Gospels next to it. Jesus begins his preaching, in Matthew, with "the kingdom of heaven is at hand." There it is, in the second line. He feeds crowds with a few loaves. There's the bread. He forgives sinners and tells a story of a father running to meet a lost son. There's the forgiveness. He's tempted in the desert, and he frees people from evil spirits. There are the last lines. The prayer runs through the Gospel like a spine. The Catechism adds a second thought from Tertullian that's practical. Jesus also said, ask and you shall receive, and everyone has needs of their own. So Tertullian says this prayer comes first, as the foundation, and the rest of our asking is built on top of it. A Catholic praying for a sick friend or a hard week isn't meant to set the Our Father aside. It goes underneath. And it's short. Short enough for a child to learn by heart, said at Mass, at a bedside, in a rosary, under the breath at a red light. Small enough to carry anywhere. Big enough, Tertullian said, to hold everything.
screen: `A SHORT SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE GOSPEL.` · `THE GOSPELS INSIDE THE PRAYER.` · `THE FOUNDATION FOR ALL ASKING.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO CARRY ANYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it very slowly. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the Our Father with one phrase on each out-breath, and let the pause between phrases be as long as the words. Our Father. Who art in heaven. Hallowed be thy name. Don't rush to the end; you may not reach it, and that's fine. If you don't pray, simply listen to the phrases one at a time, and notice which one catches. The bell holds the time.
The whole gospel in a prayer. Tertullian's description of the Our Father, which the Catechism quotes: a short summary of the whole gospel, and the foundation for all our asking. Today's words.
screen: `THE WHOLE GOSPEL IN A PRAYER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the whole gospel. Today, say the Our Father once, or just read it, and see which line of the Gospel stories it brings to mind. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass, within the rosary and the Liturgy of the Hours, and in personal prayer; families teach it to children by heart.

fork.setup: you have a sick friend and a hard week, and a long list of things to ask God for. in Tertullian's view, where does the Our Father fit?
options: say it instead of the list.
say it first, as the foundation.
fork.reveal: Tertullian, quoted in the Catechism, says the Lord's Prayer comes first, as the foundation of further desires. the personal asking builds on it.

notes: CCC 2761 paraphrased (copyrighted English). Check: Tertullian's 'summary of the whole gospel' and his second line that the Lord's Prayer is said first as the foundation of further desires, since the Lord also said 'Ask and you will receive' and each person has needs of their own.
Latin 'breviarium totius evangelii': confirm against the CCC's Latin footnote to De oratione 1. 'Near its start' for the phrase's place in De oratione; confirm.
'An early Christian writer' is the only description of Tertullian given (no dates or places, by the claims rule).
'Short enough for a child to learn by heart' and howItsDone 'families teach it to children by heart' are general observations; soften if the Keeper prefers.
Week end (days 1142–1148): the hook looks back over the week's topics.
Douay-Rheims: confirm exact wording of Matthew 6:9–10 and Matthew 4:17 ('Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand').

Editor pass: fixed 'stories of fathers running to meet lost sons' (there is one such parable, Luke 15:11–32); cut the Gethsemane 'not my will' line, which tomorrow's lesson uses as its centerpiece, and the vague 'faces evil head on', replacing them with Jesus freeing people from evil spirits (e.g. Matthew 8:16).
